description: The hand-verified expected result for the negative Opengrep SARIF fixture whose defective record hangs off an ACYCLIC originalUriBaseIds chain longer than the walk's fixed depth bound. Every value was derived by reading the fixture and the authored contracts in harness/lib/normalize/, never by running the adapter and recording what it printed. Where this file and harness/lib/normalize/adapters/sarif.py disagree, the disagreement is the finding: diagnose it rather than overwriting this file to match. It follows the key names reject-sarif-unresolvable-path.rows.json established -- rows, row_derivations, rejections, counts, counters and the negative-only routing and rejection_boundary blocks -- and adds four blocks this condition needs and no other fixture does: guard_under_test, which names the depth bound as the guard and proves the visited-identifier set cannot fire; bound_value_policy, which states why no bound value appears anywhere in this file; chain_legality, which records that the chain terminates on an absolute URI and is therefore sound data stopped by a consumer bound; and metadata_dependency, which states in full which runner-metadata context this expectation is asserted under and what the other context would produce instead.

fixture.derivation: A negative fixture is derived from the captured one rather than being an excerpt of it, so the provenance is stated as a derivation. Two of the three results are unmodified captured output: /runs/0/results/0 is canonically byte-identical to harness/artifacts/raw/opengrep.sarif results[432], to the positive fixture's results[1] and to reject-sarif-unresolvable-path.sarif results[0]; /runs/0/results/2 is canonically identical to that artifact's results[521] and the positive fixture's results[2]. The third, /runs/0/results/1, is the record the fixture points at the deep chain: it is that artifact's results[0] with exactly two differences, both established by structural comparison rather than assumed -- its artifactLocation uriBaseId is repointed from %SRCROOT% to BASE_01, and its fingerprints object is removed, so no captured fingerprint stays attached to a record whose base the fixture altered. Its ruleId, message, region and uri are the captured ones untouched, which is what leaves the chain as the only thing wrong with it.
fixture.captured_provenance: The 42-entry /runs/0/originalUriBaseIds map is the fixture's own addition: the captured artifact emits none at all -- the documented producer gap (semgrep issue 10591), recorded in harness/artifacts/logs/runner-metadata.json as sarif_original_uri_base_ids_emitted false -- so no captured artifact could have supplied a chain to walk. The three driver rules are the captured rules verbatim, at raw driver indices 529, 1283 and 1458. The recorded sha256 and byte size above are what make a later edit to the fixture visible: these values are re-derived when the fixture changes, never adjusted to keep a test green.
fixture.not_records: The three entries under /runs/0/invocations/0/toolExecutionNotifications are tool notifications -- two syntax errors and one rule timeout over vendored minified JavaScript -- and are not finding records. They are neither rows nor rejections and are not counted: a reading that counted anything finding-shaped would arrive at six records and fail the reconciliation identity for a reason that has nothing to do with the adapter. The 42 originalUriBaseIds entries are likewise not records: they are the base map the walk reads, not findings, and none of them contributes a row, a rejection or a count.

routing.detected_by: normalize.shape.is_sarif -- a version of "2.1.0" together with a runs array; those two together are the whole test
routing.routing_decision: normalize.shape.route("opengrep", doc) returns tool "opengrep", shape "sarif", adapter "sarif", scanner_class "sast"
routing.not_a_shape_failure: No normalize.shape.UnknownArtifactShape is expected here, and a test asserting one against this fixture would be asserting the wrong thing. The enclosing document is valid SARIF 2.1.0 and routes cleanly; exactly one record inside it names a base whose chain the walk will not follow to the end, and the adapter rejects that record while still emitting the others. The fixtures that own shape-detection failure are near-sarif-version-only.json, near-sarif-runs-only.json and unknown-shape.json.
routing.negative_routing_test: The mandated negative routing assertion -- that a native artifact must not route to the SARIF adapter -- belongs to test_shape_routing_negative.py and does not use this fixture.

field_order_authority: harness/lib/normalize/emit.py, the FIELDS constant. Every row below carries all twelve keys in that order, present-with-null rather than omitted.
absence_convention: Absence is JSON null here and in findings.json, and an empty field in findings.csv. tool, scanner_class, rule_id, message, severity_norm, path and in_scope are never absent -- exactly emit.REQUIRED_FIELDS.

allowlist.note: in_scope is decided by that file alone. The globs are not copied here: the allowlist is the single authority and stays byte-exact. The glob each row matched is recorded per row under row_derivations.

guard_under_test.guard: the depth bound of the uriBaseId chain walk
guard_under_test.guard_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, resolve_uri_base: "The walk is bounded twice over: a visited-identifier set stops a cycle on the repeat, and max_depth stops a chain that is merely too long." This fixture exercises the second of those two guards and cannot reach the first.
guard_under_test.visited_set_cannot_fire_evidence: Every one of the 42 keys under /runs/0/originalUriBaseIds is distinct, and the identifiers the defective record's chain walks -- BASE_01, each entry naming the next, through to the entry that carries no uriBaseId -- are distinct from one another and from %SRCROOT% and %PROJECTROOT%. Verified by walking the map from BASE_01 and comparing the identifiers collected against their own set, not by reading the fixture's naming scheme and assuming it. No identifier can therefore be revisited, so resolve_uri_base's cycle branch is unreachable on this fixture and the depth bound is the only guard that can stop the walk.
guard_under_test.expected_walk_outcome_authority: paths.BASE_OUTCOME_OVER_DEPTH, a member of the closed set paths.BASE_OUTCOMES
guard_under_test.walk_outcome_is_metadata_independent: resolve_uri_base is given only the identifier and the run's originalUriBaseIds map, so which terminal case it reports is a property of the fixture alone and no runner metadata can change it. That is the sense in which this diagnosis is unconditional. What the metadata does decide is the resolver's disposition of that outcome, which metadata_dependency below states in full rather than leaving to be discovered.
guard_under_test.why_separate_from_the_cycle_fixture: reject-sarif-uribaseid-cycle.sarif owns the visited-identifier set and this fixture owns the depth bound, and neither can stand in for the other. A cyclic chain never reaches the depth branch, because the repeat fires first; an acyclic chain never reaches the visited branch, because nothing repeats. Both produce the same reject class -- unresolvable_path -- and only the walk outcome carried in the detail tells them apart, so a test that asserted the class alone would pass against either fixture while leaving one of the two guards entirely unexercised. That is the reason these two fixtures exist separately, and it is the reason this file asserts the detail's distinguishing substrings alongside the class.

bound_value_policy.bound_reference: paths.SARIF_BASE_CHAIN_MAX_DEPTH -- referenced by name throughout this file and nowhere by value
bound_value_policy.reason: The requirement is that the walk is bounded, not that the bound is any particular number. An expected file naming the bound would keep passing while testing nothing the day paths.py chose a larger one, and would have to be edited for a change that is not a change in behaviour. Nothing in this file is a function of the bound's value.
bound_value_policy.chain_identifiers_note: The fixture's own census, measured by walking /runs/0/originalUriBaseIds from BASE_01 to the entry that carries no uriBaseId. It is the size of the fixture, not the bound, and no expectation here is derived from it; it is recorded because a reader hand-verifying this file needs to see that the chain is deliberately far beyond any plausible bound rather than marginally over one.
bound_value_policy.assertion_form: Assert the reject class exactly, and the detail by the bound-free substrings listed under rejections[0].expected_detail_substrings. Full-string equality on the detail is wrong here: the rendered detail embeds both the bound's value and the identifiers visited before it was reached, and both of those change if the bound changes.

chain_legality.evidence: Read from /runs/0/originalUriBaseIds/BASE_40, the entry the walk from BASE_01 arrives at last: it carries an absolute file: URI and no uriBaseId, so the chain terminates rather than dangling or looping. Every intermediate entry carries a relative uri and a uriBaseId naming the next identifier, and every one of those identifiers has an entry, so no level of the chain is dangling either.
chain_legality.diagnosis_note: Given unlimited depth this chain would resolve correctly: resolve_uri_base accumulates each relative level and joins them beneath the first absolute ancestor, so the walk would come to rest under the terminal file: URI with the chain's relative segments joined below it, and the record would take a path under that. The producer's data is sound and the consumer's bound is what stopped the walk. AAP 0.5.4 requires each terminal case be reportable as itself, and this is the case where nothing is malformed.
chain_legality.why_that_distinction_matters: A reader of tool-status.md deciding whether to raise a bound or to report a producer defect needs exactly this distinction, and a rejection recorded only as unresolvable_path answers neither question. It is also what separates this fixture from reject-sarif-uribaseid-relative-no-absolute-ancestor.sarif, whose chain ends on a relative reference with no absolute ancestor and therefore could not resolve at any depth.

resolution_context.root_independence: All three uris in the fixture are root-relative, and the two that resolve do so through their own base chain rather than through any recorded base, so these rows hold for whatever absolute scan root the adapter is given as long as the fixture's terminal base names it. No absolute path appears anywhere in this file. The rejected record is root-independent for a different reason: the walk stops before any base exists to join it onto, so no choice of root could change the outcome.
resolution_context.path_base_note: The asserted context, stated rather than assumed. metadata_dependency below gives the authority for it and records what the other context produces instead.
resolution_context.surviving_records_walk_note: %SRCROOT% names a relative uri with a uriBaseId of %PROJECTROOT%, whose uri is absolute -- the two-level chain of SARIF 2.1.0 section 3.14.14's own example, expressed relative to its parent exactly as the specification shows. The walk therefore completes within any bound and the surviving rows never depend on the runner-recorded base at all.
resolution_context.path_basis_authority: paths.BASIS_SARIF_BASE_CHAIN -- the basis for a relative reference resolved through a completed uriBaseId walk, which is what both surviving rows take. Neither surviving row takes paths.BASIS_SARIF_METADATA_BASE, because neither needed a fallback.
resolution_context.severity_source: Neither surviving result states a level of its own, and no rule carries properties.severity or properties.problem.severity, so each severity_native is the level its own rule states under defaultConfiguration.level -- SARIF 2.1.0's own derivation for a result that omits the property -- and each severity_norm comes from the SARIF level table: error High, warning Medium, note Low, none Info.
resolution_context.package_coordinate: null on every row. A SARIF result names a code location rather than a package, and this shape supplies no coordinate to carry.

metadata_dependency.statement: The walk outcome is fixture-determined; what the resolver then does with an over-depth outcome is decided by the runner metadata, and this file names which of the two contexts it asserts. paths.BASE_OUTCOMES_ELIGIBLE_FOR_METADATA_FALLBACK carries over-depth alongside absent, cycle and degenerate, so resolve_sarif_location rejects an over-depth record only where the metadata supplies no explicit base for the tool, and resolves it through the runner-recorded base where one is recorded.
metadata_dependency.aap_authority: AAP 0.5.4, case 1: a base identifier absent from originalUriBaseIds, or a chain that cycles or exceeds the depth, "resolves through the runner-recorded base only where the runner metadata supplies an explicit base for that tool, and is otherwise a rejection under unresolvable_path", together with "The documented degenerate-base fallback is not a catch-all -- it applies where the metadata makes the base known, and everywhere else the record is rejected and counted rather than guessed."

asserted_context.authority: paths.ToolPathBase.has_explicit_base is kind != "none" and a non-empty base value, so the "none" kind is false by construction. paths.PATH_BASE_KINDS carries "none", and the runner-metadata document annotates it: paths.py must reject such a record under unresolvable_path rather than fall back.
asserted_context.outcome: rows 2, rejections 1, rejections_by_class {unresolvable_path: 1}, parse_status partial -- the expectation the rows, rejections, counts and counters blocks below assert.
asserted_context.why_this_is_the_asserted_one: It is the only context in which the depth bound is observable as an outcome. Under an explicit base the walk still reports over-depth, but the record becomes a row and nothing in the dataset or the counts distinguishes it from a record that resolved normally -- so a test run under that context would assert a passing artifact while the guard it exists to cover went unexercised. AAP 0.9.4 requires a negative fixture and an assertion for every rejection condition an adapter can produce, and over-depth-with-no-explicit-base is that condition for this fixture.

alternative_context.provenance: harness/artifacts/logs/runner-metadata.json records exactly this for opengrep -- path_base.kind scan_root with the pinned scan root as its value -- so this is the context the production pipeline resolves opengrep under, not a hypothetical.
alternative_context.outcome: rows 3, rejections 0, parse_status clean. The defective record resolves through the documented fallback on basis paths.BASIS_SARIF_METADATA_BASE and becomes a row: rule_id opt.blitzy-harness.rules.opengrep-rules.java.lang.correctness.hardcoded-conditional, message "This if statement will always have the same behavior and is therefore unnecessary.", severity_native error, severity_norm High, path common/network-common/src/main/java/org/apache/spark/network/buffer/FileSegmentManagedBuffer.java, start_line 112, cwe null, cve null, package_coordinate null, in_scope true. Its ResolvedPath carries a corroboration naming the over-depth outcome and the base it was resolved through, so even there the walk's failure is recorded rather than lost.
alternative_context.corroboration: That row is field-for-field the row expected/opengrep.rows.json carries at index 0 for the same captured record, which is what makes this branch a measured statement rather than a projection.
alternative_context.why_recorded: Because a test author reaching for opengrep's real metadata would otherwise see a rejection expectation fail and read it as an adapter defect. The two contexts differ in one recorded flag, both outcomes are correct for their context, and naming both is what keeps the disagreement from looking like one.

metadata_dependency.unconditional_diagnoses_for_contrast: Two of the five uriBaseId diagnoses are unconditional in the stronger sense that no metadata can rescue them: no-absolute-ancestor, which resolve_sarif_location rejects before the fallback is considered because it is absent from BASE_OUTCOMES_ELIGIBLE_FOR_METADATA_FALLBACK, and invalid-uri, which it rejects under a different class entirely. Over-depth is not one of those two, and recording it as though it were would misstate paths.py.

uri_base_id_diagnoses.why_kept_separate: A reader of tool-status.md needs to know why a path failed to resolve, not merely that it did. All five diagnoses reach the same record-level conclusion -- no path, so no row -- and four of them are reported under the same reject class, so the class alone would collapse five different producer or consumer conditions into one number. paths.py keeps them distinct as BASE_OUTCOME_* values carried in the rejection detail, and this tree keeps one fixture per diagnosis so each is exercised by something.

diagnoses.condition: the identifier the record names has no entry in originalUriBaseIds, or the run emits no map at all
the chain revisits an identifier, so the visited-identifier set stops the walk
the chain is acyclic and legal but longer than the bound, so the depth guard stops the walk -- this file's fixture
the chain terminates on a relative reference with no uriBaseId to resolve it against, so no depth would help
an entry in the chain is not an artifactLocation object, or its uri is not a valid URI reference -- the one diagnosis of the five that is not reported under unresolvable_path

uri_base_id_diagnoses.sixth_outcome_note: paths.BASE_OUTCOMES carries one further non-resolved member, degenerate -- a base naming the filesystem root, an archive member or a foreign scheme, the trivy issue 10364 shape -- and no fixture in this tree is named for it. Recorded so its absence from the five is visible rather than looking like an oversight in this list.

rejection_boundary.statement: A path that cannot be resolved is a rejection. A path that merely resolves somewhere unwanted is a kept row with in_scope false. This fixture's defective record resolves to nothing, because the walk that would have produced its base stopped before reaching one -- which is what makes it the unresolvable_path case rather than one of the three kept cases below.
rejection_boundary.why_it_can_only_be_a_rejection: path is one of only two never-absent fields in the twelve-field schema, the other being severity_norm: emit.REQUIRED_FIELDS carries path, and emit.OPTIONAL_FIELDS is exactly severity_native, start_line, cwe, cve and package_coordinate. A record with no resolvable path therefore has no valid row representation at all -- emit.py raises on a null path rather than writing one -- so counting it under a named class is the only outcome that neither drops the record nor invents a coordinate for it.
rejection_boundary.scope_is_not_why_it_is_rejected: The defective record's uri is common/network-common/src/main/java/org/apache/spark/network/buffer/FileSegmentManagedBuffer.java, which matches the allowlist glob common/network-common/src/main/** and carries no src/test segment: had its chain resolved, it would have been an in-scope row. Stated because a reader could otherwise read the rejection as a scope decision, and in_scope is never why a record is rejected.

not_a_rejection.case: a path resolving outside the twelve authoritative globs
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope false, counted under rows_out_of_scope
not_a_rejection.evidence: The real out-of-glob files in the pinned tree are dev/package-lock.json, ui-test/package-lock.json and docs/Gemfile.lock. Each resolves to a tree_file path and is kept; out of scope means kept and marked, never rejected.

not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope false, counted in non_filesystem_paths
not_a_rejection.evidence: Serialized as <container-relative-to-root>!<member> with ! the single separator, and with ../ segments preserved rather than normalized where the container lies outside the root -- the SARIF 2.1.0 errata forbid a consumer normalizing .. segments out of a path.

not_a_rejection.case: a path in a src/test tree
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope false
not_a_rejection.evidence: The exclusion is literal -- a path containing src/test is out of scope -- and it removes the path from scope rather than from the dataset. Row 1 below is the near case that proves the rule is literal: it is a Python test module under python/pyspark/, it carries no src/test segment, and it is in scope.

rejection_boundary.no_guessed_path: The rejected record is rejected and counted, never given a path. Nothing in this file supplies a coordinate for it under the asserted context, not even the one its chain would have produced at unlimited depth.

counts.raw_count_unit: one element of runs[].results[] -- the unit normalize.reconcile.count_records walks independently of row construction
counts.raw_count_authority: normalize.reconcile.count_records("opengrep", doc), whose SARIF traversal sums the length of each run's results array and builds no row, resolves no path and maps no severity. It is the independent half of the identity: a count taken from the traversal that builds the rows would satisfy the assertion while testing nothing. Measured over this fixture it is 3, and it is unaffected by which metadata context the adapter is given -- the left-hand side of the identity is the same under both branches, and only the split between rows and rejections moves.

four_reported_counters.authority: AAP 0.5.4 -- the four counts reported per tool
four_reported_counters.note: Named here rather than restated with their values. The counters block below is the single measurement, and a number carried twice inside one document is a number that can drift; counters_note gives the reason each of the four is zero.

counts.parse_status_authority: harness/lib/normalize/cli.py, PARSE_STATUS_PARTIAL = "partial", assigned as partial where there are rejections and clean where there are none. Partial is right precisely because the adapter did not abandon the artifact: every parsable record was emitted and the one rejected record is counted under its class, with its reason retained. This is deliberately not normalize.reconcile's STATUS_PASS / STATUS_FAIL / STATUS_NOT_APPLICABLE vocabulary, which describes an assertion's outcome rather than an artifact's parse.

counters_authority: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/sarif.py, COUNTER_KEYS as returned by new_counters(): twenty authored keys, one path_kind_* per paths.PATH_KINDS member and one severity_basis_* per severity.BASIS_VALUES member, twenty-nine in total.
counters_note: Three things a reader must not "correct". First, rule_id_from_rule_id is 3 while the severity counters are 2: the rule step is step 2 of the adapter's classification order and the path step is step 4, so the rejected record resolves its rule identifier before it is rejected and never reaches severity. That asymmetry is the classification order made visible, not a miscount. Second, the four counters AAP 0.5.4 has reported per tool are all 0 here: every result carries exactly one location, so multi_location_records is 0; each rule that names a weakness names exactly one, so multi_valued_cwe_records is 0; no rule string carries a CVE identifier, so multi_valued_cve_records is 0; and both emitted paths name a file inside the scanned tree, so non_filesystem_paths is 0. Third, there is no counter for the walk outcome and none for the depth bound: paths.py returns the outcome in the rejection detail rather than tallying it, so this block cannot be where a reader looks for evidence that the bound fired -- rejections[0] is.

corroboration.note: The two surviving results are two of the captured results the positive sibling covers -- this file's row 0 is that file's row 1, and this file's row 1 is that file's row 2 -- and all twenty-four field comparisons agree, including the two CWE selections and the two severity bands. Recorded after the fact rather than as the source of these values: each value here was derived from the fixture and the authored contracts, so a future disagreement between this file and the adapter is a finding to diagnose rather than a diff to apply. The rejected record's counterpart in that file, its row 0, is what the alternative context under metadata_dependency would produce here, which is why that branch could be stated as a measurement instead of a projection.
corroboration.path_basis_differs_from_the_positive_sib: Deliberate and not a discrepancy. The positive fixture carries no originalUriBaseIds, so its rows resolve through the runner-recorded base on basis sarif-degenerate-base-metadata-fallback; this fixture supplies a base map, so its rows resolve through the chain on basis sarif-uri-base-id-chain. The twelve emitted fields are identical either way -- the basis is provenance for how the path was reached, and it is not one of the twelve.

rows.message: User data flows into this manually-constructed SQL string. User data can be safely inserted into SQL strings using prepared statements or an object-relational mapper (ORM). Manually-constructed SQL strings is a possible indicator of SQL injection, which could let an attacker steal or manipulate data from the database. Instead, use prepared statements (`connection.PreparedStatement`) or a safe library.

Avoid using `pickle`, which is known to lead to code execution vulnerabilities. When unpickling, the serialized data could be manipulated to run arbitrary code. Instead, consider serializing the relevant data as JSON or a similar text-based serialization format.

row_derivations.rule_id_source: the result's own ruleId; no ruleIndex and no rule reference is present
row_derivations.severity_native_note: the result states no level of its own, so the level is the one its rule states -- SARIF 2.1.0's own derivation, not an inference

cwe_source.text: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')

row_derivations.anchor_note: The contrast row this fixture exists to keep: its base sits outside the deep chain, so it resolves while the record on that chain does not, and the adapter is shown rejecting one record selectively rather than abandoning the artifact. Line 72 of the pinned DiskStore.scala is the interpolated string argument of the SparkException.internalError(...) call that opens on line 71, and the file is 380 lines, so start_line is within the file.

row_derivations.rule_id_source: the result's own ruleId; no ruleIndex and no rule reference is present
row_derivations.severity_native_note: the result states no level of its own, so the level is the one its rule states -- SARIF 2.1.0's own derivation, not an inference
row_derivations.anchor_note: The second surviving row, from a different module, a different language and a different severity band, so the fixture proves the adapter carried on past the rejected record rather than merely emitting the one that preceded it. It is also the literal-exclusion case: a Python test module inside the authoritative glob, carrying no src/test segment, in scope and scanned. Line 90 of the pinned file is the pickle.load(f) call, and the file is 219 lines.

rejections.locator_note: The pointer and the run_index / result_index pair name the same record. The pair is carried as well because normalize.adapters.sarif passes exactly run_index, result_index and rule_id into the rejection it builds, so a produced Rejection's record_identity and this expectation can be compared directly, without translating one coordinate system into the other.
rejections.reject_class_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, the REJECT_UNRESOLVABLE_PATH constant -- a literal member of paths.REJECT_CLASSES, the closed set of ten. Written verbatim rather than paraphrased, and asserted against the module rather than by eye: a test that only counts rejections cannot tell one condition from another, so the class name is what carries the assertion, and here even the class is not enough on its own -- see guard_under_test.why_separate_from_the_cycle_fixture.
rejections.classification_step: step 4 of the adapter's fixed classification order -- shape, rule identifier, message, path, start_line. Steps 1 to 3 all pass on this record: it is a JSON object, it carries a valid ruleId that resolves to /runs/0/tool/driver/rules/0, and it carries a non-empty message.text. That is deliberate, so the only thing left to reject it for is its path.
rejections.start_line_never_examined: Step 5 is never reached, so this record's region.startLine of 112 is never examined and non_integer_start_line is not in play. Worth stating because the fixture does give the defective record a startLine -- the captured one, an integer and valid -- and a reader could otherwise expect an interaction between the two conditions.
rejections.uri_form_authority: paths.parse_uri_reference classifies a reference with no scheme and no leading slash as URI_FORM_RELATIVE, which is the one form that needs a base -- so the record reaches the uriBaseId walk rather than being classified before it. Contrast reject-sarif-unresolvable-path.sarif, whose foreign-scheme uri is rejected before any base is resolved.
rejections.walk_guard_that_could_not_fire: the visited-identifier set -- every identifier in the chain is distinct, so no repeat exists for it to catch
expected_detail_substrings: uriBaseId chain exceeds the bound of
documented degenerate-base fallback does not apply
rejected rather than resolved through a guess
rejections.expected_detail_shape: The rendered detail is the walk's own detail -- naming the uriBaseId chain, the bound it exceeded and the identifiers visited before it did -- followed by resolve_sarif_location's metadata clause, which names the recorded path_base.kind and states that the documented fallback therefore does not apply. Assert the substrings above, never the whole string: the bound's value and the visited identifiers both appear in it and both change with the bound, which is exactly the coupling bound_value_policy refuses.
rejections.expected_detail_note: The detail is the sub-reason AAP 0.5.4 requires a rejection to carry, and it is the only place the diagnosis lives: unresolvable_path covers a base that was absent, one that cycled, one that was over-depth, one that was degenerate with no recorded base, and a chain with no absolute ancestor. Naming the class alone would not distinguish this record from any of the other four.
rejections.record_identity_note: The adapter supplies run_index, result_index and rule_id; the resolver adds the raw uri and, where one is present as a non-empty string, the raw uriBaseId. Enough to find the record in the artifact again, and never the record itself and never a secret value.
rejections.why_not_a_row: There is no path to put in the row. The walk stopped before producing a base, and under the asserted context no recorded base may stand in for it, so nothing can be joined onto and path -- never absent from a row -- has no value. Dropping the record or giving it a guessed path would each hide it; counting it under a named class keeps it visible and keeps the arithmetic honest.
rejections.contributes_no_severity_literal: The rejected record is never fed to the severity tally, so the error literal its rule states never reaches severity-map.md from this fixture. That document reports literals against the rows the dataset contains, and this record contributes none.
rejections.under_the_alternative_context: This same record becomes a row rather than a rejection where the runner metadata supplies an explicit base; metadata_dependency.alternative_context states that row in full. The walk outcome is over-depth in both cases -- what changes is only whether the resolver may fall back.

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: shape-detection failure -- an artifact matching neither SARIF nor a known native shape halting the run
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.why_absent: this document is valid SARIF 2.1.0 and routes cleanly; its defect is one record's base chain, not its shape

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: the visited-identifier guard of the uriBaseId walk
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.why_absent: every identifier in this fixture's chain is distinct, which is the property that makes the depth bound the only guard able to fire here -- and the reason the two fixtures are separate rather than one

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: the three uriBaseId diagnoses this fixture does not produce -- absent, no-absolute-ancestor and invalid-uri
